reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A common benign epithelial ovarian tumour lined by tubal-type serous epithelium and filled with thin, watery fluid
Usually presents in reproductive-age and perimenopausal women as an asymptomatic cyst or with vague pelvic pressure
Typically a thin-walled, unilocular cyst with clear fluid and few or no septations on ultrasound, and is bilateral in a proportion of cases
Psammoma bodies (concentric calcifications) may be present histologically
Distinguished from borderline and malignant serous tumours by the absence of epithelial proliferation, atypia, and stromal invasion
Complications are mechanical, chiefly torsion or rupture, rather than invasive spread
Managed by observation for small simple cysts or by cystectomy or oophorectomy when large, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain
reference.pathophysiology: Serous cystadenomas are benign surface-epithelial tumours whose lining recapitulates the ciliated, tubal-type epithelium of the fallopian tube, reflecting the current understanding that many serous ovarian tumours derive from tubal or Mullerian epithelium. The epithelium is a single, orderly layer without the stratification, tufting, or cytological atypia seen in borderline and malignant counterparts, and there is no stromal invasion. Secretion of serous fluid by this epithelium produces a thin-walled cyst, and concentric calcified psammoma bodies may form. Because growth is non-invasive, clinical problems arise from the size of the cyst and mechanical events such as torsion or rupture rather than from local or distant spread.
additionalDifferentials: Serous borderline tumour or low-grade serous carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to characterise a thin-walled unilocular cyst
Pelvic MRI when the lesion is large or indeterminate
CA125 and risk-of-malignancy assessment to help stratify the lesion
Serial ultrasound follow-up for small simple cysts
Histology to confirm a benign lining and exclude a borderline or malignant component
Doppler assessment if torsion is suspected
redFlags: Solid or papillary components, thick septations, or ascites suggesting a borderline or malignant tumour
Acute pain indicating torsion or rupture
Rapid enlargement of a previously stable cyst
A markedly raised CA125 in a complex adnexal mass
reference.prognosis: Excellent, as serous cystadenomas are benign and cured by complete excision, with no tendency to invasive spread; recurrence is uncommon and usually represents a new lesion.
pitfalls: Assuming any serous cystic lesion is benign and missing a borderline or malignant tumour
Rupturing or incompletely excising a cyst and prompting recurrence
Over-relying on a normal CA125, which is frequently normal even in benign disease and can be raised for non-neoplastic reasons
Overlooking torsion as a cause of acute presentation
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Manage a confidently benign simple cyst conservatively with serial ultrasound surveillance in appropriate women
Undertake surgical removal by fertility-sparing ovarian cystectomy or oophorectomy for large, symptomatic, or indeterminate lesions, preferring a laparoscopic approach that minimises rupture
Stratify malignant risk before surgery using CA125 and the risk-of-malignancy index
Manage acute torsion or cyst rupture as a surgical emergency
Confirm the benign serous lining on histology to exclude a borderline or malignant component
Refer to gynaecology for planning of surveillance versus surgery
